fields.expected:
I'm an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins studying Applied Mathematics & Statistics and Economics, and the work most relevant to an AI and automation internship is a browser-automation agent I built for the job search itself.

The problem was that applying to jobs is mostly repetitive browser work: opening ATS pages, refilling the same information, tracking state, following up. But fully autonomous browser agents are dangerous there, because one wrong action submits a real application or fills a legal field incorrectly. So I built it in TypeScript and Node with Playwright, using SQLite as the single source of truth because automation gets unsafe when application state diverges across processes. Every application moves through an explicit state machine, from DISCOVERED through FILL to SUBMITTED, and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED that never default on. Free-text and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from auto-fill and always generate a human-review item. Greenhouse is supported end to end; Workday and iCIMS are detected and deliberately skipped rather than handled unreliably.

That's how I think about automation: deciding where it should stop matters as much as where it can go.
